0.title: Obadiah: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
0.overview:
Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament: one chapter, twenty-one verses. We know nothing at all about the prophet apart from his name. He gives us no king, no date and no family, only The vision of Obadiah (v. 1). Yet this small book asks a question every believer eventually asks. What does God do about the people who stood by, or even cheered, while his people suffered?

The message concerns Edom, and to understand it you need to know that Edom and Israel were family. The Edomites descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob. The conflict began before the brothers were born, when God said to their mother, Two nations are in your womb (Gen 25:23). Esau sold his birthright, lost his father's blessing and hated Jacob (Gen 27:41). The two men themselves were later reconciled, and Esau embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him (Gen 33:4). But their descendants nursed the quarrel for a thousand years, even though God's law told Israel, You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deut 23:7).

Then came the day Jerusalem fell. Enemy soldiers broke through the gates, looted the city and gambled for what was left, and Edom stood on the hillside and watched. Worse, they cheered, looted alongside the invaders, and caught the refugees who were running for their lives. Psalm 137 remembers it with tears: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem (Ps 137:7). Obadiah is God's answer.

Christians differ about when Obadiah preached. Most place him soon after 586 BC, when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, since verses 11-14 read like an eyewitness account of that disaster. Others place him in the ninth century BC, when Edom rebelled against Judah and raiders plundered the city. Much of the book also runs closely parallel to Jeremiah 49:7-22, and we cannot be sure which prophet wrote first, or whether both drew on an older oracle. Happily, nothing in the message depends on these questions.

The book falls into three parts. Verses 1-9 announce Edom's fall and expose its cause: The pride of your heart has deceived you (v. 3). Edom lived in cliff fortresses in the red rock country southeast of the Dead Sea and felt untouchable, asking, Who will bring me down to the ground? God replies that however high the eagle nests, he reaches higher. Verses 10-14 bring the charge: the violence done to your brother Jacob. Edom stood aloof, and God's verdict on the bystander is devastating: you were like one of them (v. 11). Eight commands follow, tracing how sin grows from a gloating look to robbery and murder. Verses 15-21 lift the horizon to the day of the LORD upon all the nations, and end with rescue on Mount Zion and the promise that the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

Three themes run through the book. Pride deceives. Edom's confidence was built on geography, wealth, clever advisers and strong allies, and God removed all four. God watches how we treat one another. The sins named here are not exotic: looking on, feeling pleased, saying something, then joining in. God repays. The rule of his day is As you have done, it shall be done to you (v. 15). Jesus said the same: with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt 7:2).

That last theme would leave us all without hope, because none of us could survive a judgment that handed back exactly what we have given others. This is why Obadiah's picture of a cup matters so much (v. 16). The prophets often describe God's judgment as a cup the nations must drink. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39). At the cross he received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. He is also the fulfilment of the book's last promise. Obadiah says Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion (v. 21); the New Testament tells believers, you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb 12:22, 24). At the end the announcement rings out, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (Rev 11:15).

Obadiah's severity toward a nation is not God's last word to individuals from that nation. Amos heard God promise that the restored kingdom of David would include the remnant of Edom (Amos 9:12), and the apostles saw that promise coming true as Gentiles turned to Christ (Acts 15:16-17). There is a striking footnote to the story. Centuries after Obadiah, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matt 2:16). Esau's line made one last attempt on Jacob's, and failed. Edom has vanished from history; the King they tried to kill reigns forever, and people from every nation belong to him.

So this little book speaks to anyone who has been wronged and wondered whether God noticed, and to anyone tempted to enjoy an enemy's downfall. Do not be proud, for God brings the high down. Do not gloat, for God is watching how we treat our brothers. And do not be afraid of the powers that look unshakeable, because the last word of Obadiah is also the last word of history: the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Pride of Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God announces war on Edom: Behold, I will make you small among the nations (vv. 1-2). The pride of your heart has deceived you, says the LORD to the people safe in their rock fortresses; though they nest among the stars, he will bring them down (vv. 3-4). Thieves leave something behind, but Esau will be stripped bare, betrayed by his own allies (vv. 5-7). Even Edom's famous wisdom and its soldiers will fail (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride deceives, and no height, wealth or cleverness can keep anyone safe from God.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord GOD concerning Edom: We have heard a report from the LORD, and a messenger has been sent among the nations: "Rise up! Let us rise against her for battle!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord GOD concerning Edom: We have heard a report from the LORD, and a messenger has been sent among the nations: "Rise up! Let us rise against her for battle!"

Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, twenty-one verses, and we know nothing about the man who wrote it except his name. He tells us no king, no date and no family. What we have is simply The vision of Obadiah, a message he received from God concerning Edom.

Christians hold two main views about when he preached. Most believe it was soon after 586 BC, when the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem, because verses 11-14 describe foreigners entering the gates and casting lots for the city while Edom looked on. Psalm 137 remembers that day and prays, Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem (Ps 137:7). Others believe he preached much earlier, in the ninth century BC, when Edom rebelled against Judah (2 Kgs 8:20-22) and raiders plundered Jerusalem and the royal household (2 Chr 21:16-17). Nothing in the message depends on settling it.

Readers often notice that much of Obadiah is very like Jeremiah 49:7-22. Some think Jeremiah drew on Obadiah, some the reverse, and others that both used an older oracle about Edom. The message is the same either way.

Notice how the vision opens. We have heard a report from the LORD: the prophet has overheard heaven's news. A messenger has been sent among the nations, stirring them up for war against Edom. Nations imagine they choose their own wars. Obadiah shows us who is actually moving the pieces.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you shall be utterly despised. The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling, who say in your heart, "Who will bring me down to the ground?" Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you shall be utterly despised.

Edom's future is settled in one sentence. (The ESV notes that the verse may be read as already accomplished: "Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are utterly despised".) The nation that thought itself secure will become small and despised.

Who were the Edomites? They were the descendants of Esau, Jacob's twin brother (Gen 36:1). The feud began before the twins were born, when God said, Two nations are in your womb (Gen 25:23). Esau sold his birthright, lost the blessing, and hated Jacob (Gen 27:41). The brothers were later reconciled, and Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him (Gen 33:4). But their descendants kept the quarrel alive for a thousand years. Edom refused Israel passage on the way to the promised land (Num 20:18), even though God's law said, You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deut 23:7).

The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling, who say in your heart, "Who will bring me down to the ground?"

Here is the heart of the matter: The pride of your heart has deceived you. Pride is a liar. It tells us we are safe, self-sufficient and beyond correction, and by the time we discover otherwise it is too late.

Edom's pride had a geographical basis. The people lived in the clefts of the rock (the ESV notes this may be a place name, "Sela", meaning a rock stronghold), in the high red sandstone country southeast of the Dead Sea. Their settlements were perched on cliffs and reached through narrow gorges; the famous rock city of Petra, carved by a later people, lies in that region. Edom's homes looked unconquerable. So they said, Who will bring me down to the ground? It is one thing to feel secure; it is another to say in your heart that nobody, not even God, can touch you.

Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD.

God answers their question. However high the eagle builds, God reaches higher. The same charge was laid against Babylon, whose king said, I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high (Isa 14:13). Height is no defence when God is the one who brings you down.

Every reader needs this. Our fortresses are usually not cliffs but savings, qualifications, reputation, health or family. None of them are wrong in themselves, and all of them can quietly become the answer to the question "Who will bring me down?" God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Jesus said, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 18:14). It is far better to come down willingly now than to be brought down at the last.

verseByVerse.quote: If thieves came to you, if plunderers came by night— how you have been destroyed!— would they not steal only enough for themselves? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? How Esau has been pillaged, his treasures sought out! All your allies have driven you to your border; those at peace with you have deceived you; they have prevailed against you; those who eat your bread have set a trap beneath you— you have no understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If thieves came to you, if plunderers came by night— how you have been destroyed!— would they not steal only enough for themselves? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings?

How Esau has been pillaged, his treasures sought out!

Obadiah uses two pictures from ordinary life. Thieves take what they can carry and leave the rest; grape pickers always miss a few bunches, and the poor came behind to gather them. Even a robbery and a harvest leave something behind. But when God deals with Edom, nothing will be left. Their hidden treasures, stored in caves and cliff strongholds, will be sought out. The prophet breaks into the middle of his own sentence with a cry: how you have been destroyed! He speaks as if it has already happened, because God has said it.

All your allies have driven you to your border; those at peace with you have deceived you; they have prevailed against you; those who eat your bread have set a trap beneath you— you have no understanding.

Edom sat on important trade routes and knew how to make friends with the strong. Now those friends turn on them. The ones at the dinner table, those who eat your bread, set the trap. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of this line is compressed, so that the words those who eat are supplied, and that it reads "he has set a trap".) Edom, who betrayed a brother, is betrayed by friends. In time Edom was indeed driven out of its ancient territory by other peoples and had to settle further west.

The last phrase is cutting: you have no understanding. Edom was famous for its clever men, and its cleverness did not see this coming. Worldly shrewdness can arrange everything except an answer to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Will I not on that day, declares the LORD, destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of Mount Esau? And your mighty men shall be dismayed, O Teman, so that every man from Mount Esau will be cut off by slaughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will I not on that day, declares the LORD, destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of Mount Esau?

Edom had a reputation for wisdom. Jeremiah asks, Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jer 49:7), and Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite, from Edomite territory (Job 2:11). Their counsellors were respected across the region. God says he will simply remove it. Wisdom is his gift, and he can withdraw it. A nation can lose the ability to think clearly about its own danger, and it happens more often than we like to admit.

And your mighty men shall be dismayed, O Teman, so that every man from Mount Esau will be cut off by slaughter.

If the wise men cannot save Edom, perhaps the soldiers can. But the mighty men will be dismayed, their courage gone before the battle. Edom had three defences: their cliffs, their cleverness and their army. God takes away all three. It is a sober picture of what happens when God finally deals with human pride: not a fair fight, but a quiet collapse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Day of Your Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge is named: Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob (v. 10). On the day Jerusalem fell, Edom stood aloof, and was like one of them (v. 11). Then comes a drumbeat of commands: do not gloat, do not rejoice, do not boast, do not enter, do not loot, do not cut off the fugitives (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Standing by while others suffer, and gloating over a brother's ruin, are sins God takes personally.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever. On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever.

Now we learn why. The word Because introduces the charge, and the key word in it is brother. Edom and Israel were not strangers; they were family. God had protected Edom's land when Israel marched to Canaan, and had forbidden Israel to despise them. So the violence Edom did was violence against your brother Jacob.

God notices what families and churches do to their own. The closer the tie, the deeper the wound, and the more seriously he takes it.

On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.

Here is the scene: Jerusalem has fallen. Foreign soldiers pour through the broken gates, carry off everything of value and gamble for the city as if it were a prize. And where was Edom? You stood aloof. They did not swing a sword in that sentence. They simply stood and watched their brother being destroyed.

Then comes the verdict: you were like one of them. In God's eyes the bystander had joined the attackers. Standing aside is a choice. It was the sin of the priest and the Levite who crossed the road and left the wounded man (Luke 10:31-32), and it is the sin John describes when he asks how God's love can be in a person who sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him (1 John 3:17). Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (Jas 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: But do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune; do not rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their ruin; do not boast in the day of distress. Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; do not gloat over his disaster in the day of his calamity; do not loot his wealth in the day of his calamity. Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives; do not hand over his survivors in the day of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune; do not rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their ruin; do not boast in the day of distress.

Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; do not gloat over his disaster in the day of his calamity; do not loot his wealth in the day of his calamity.

Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives; do not hand over his survivors in the day of distress.

Eight commands come one after another, and the word day beats through them like a drum. God is not giving Edom advice for next time. He is naming, one by one, the things they actually did, and each command is a photograph of a crime.

Watch the progression, because it is the way sin always grows. It begins in the eyes: do not gloat. Then it reaches the heart: do not rejoice. Then it comes out of the mouth: do not boast (the ESV notes the Hebrew is vivid, "do not enlarge your mouth"). Then the feet move: Do not enter the gate of my people. Then the hands take: do not loot his wealth. Finally the worst of all: standing at the crossroads to catch the refugees running for their lives, and handing the survivors over to the enemy. What began as a look ended in murder.

Notice also what God calls Judah in the middle of this: my people. Even in the hour when he was judging them, they were still his, and he was watching how others treated them.

This is the searching part of Obadiah for ordinary readers. Few of us will ever plunder a city. But the quiet pleasure at the downfall of someone we resent, the colleague who failed, the church that split, the family member whose marriage collapsed, is the very sin God names first. Scripture says plainly, Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles (Prov 24:17). The gloating heart is only the beginning, but it is a real beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you (v. 15). The nations will drink the cup, but in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape (vv. 16-17). Esau will be stubble before the fire of Jacob (v. 18), God's people will possess the land on every side (vv. 19-20), and Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not with Edom or any empire, but with salvation on Mount Zion and the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head. For as you have drunk on my holy mountain, so all the nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow, and shall be as though they had never been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head.

The message suddenly widens. Everything so far has concerned one small nation. Now Obadiah lifts his eyes: the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. Edom is a sample case. What God does to Edom, he will do to every proud and cruel power, because he is the God of the whole earth.

And the rule of that day is simple: As you have done, it shall be done to you. Edom cut off fugitives, and Edom will be cut off (v. 9). Edom looted, and Edom will be pillaged (v. 6). Jesus stated the same principle: with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt 7:2), and Paul warned, whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).

That is terrifying if we are honest about ourselves, because none of us would survive a judgment that gave us back exactly what we have given others. This is why the gospel is such good news. At the cross, Christ did not receive what he had done; he received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved.

For as you have drunk on my holy mountain, so all the nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow, and shall be as though they had never been.

The word drunk may look back to Edom celebrating on my holy mountain, God's temple hill, while Jerusalem burned; it is a picture of revelling in another's ruin. It may also point forward to the cup of God's wrath that the prophets often describe: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine (Ps 75:8), which God made the nations drink (Jer 25:15-17). Most likely both are in view: they drank in triumph, and now they will drink judgment. The end is total: they will be as though they had never been.

There is only one way for anyone to escape that cup, and it is that Someone else drank it. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39), and then said, shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? (John 18:11). He drank it to the dregs for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions. The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no survivor for the house of Esau, for the LORD has spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions.

But is one of the great words of the Bible. Judgment is not the last word. In Mount Zion there shall be those who escape: on the hill where Edom had celebrated, God will keep a rescued people. Joel had said the same: in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape (Joel 2:32), and he added the promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved.

Zion shall be holy, cleansed of everything that defiled it, and God's people will get back what was taken from them. Christians read this with the New Testament open: you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb 12:22, 24).

The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no survivor for the house of Esau, for the LORD has spoken.

The picture is a field of dry stubble after harvest, which a single flame will destroy in minutes. Edom had seemed as permanent as its cliffs; before God's people it will prove as flimsy as straw. The house of Jacob and the house of Joseph are the southern and northern tribes together, reunited in God's purpose.

These are hard words, and honesty requires us to feel their weight. They are God's sentence on a nation that had shown no mercy, and Edom did eventually disappear as a people. Yet even here the door is not shut against individual Edomites. Amos, preaching a century or more before, heard God promise a restored kingdom of David that would include the remnant of Edom (Amos 9:12), and the apostles saw that promise fulfilled as Gentiles came to faith in Jesus (Acts 15:16-17). The nation that fought God's people perished; sinners from every nation, including Israel's old enemies, are welcomed in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau, and those of the Shephelah shall possess the land of the Philistines; they shall possess the land of Ephraim and the land of Samaria, and Benjamin shall possess Gilead. The exiles of this host of the people of Israel shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad shall possess the cities of the Negeb. Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau, and those of the Shephelah shall possess the land of the Philistines; they shall possess the land of Ephraim and the land of Samaria, and Benjamin shall possess Gilead.

The exiles of this host of the people of Israel shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad shall possess the cities of the Negeb.

These verses sweep around the compass. The Negeb is the dry south, the Shephelah the low hills west toward Philistia, Ephraim and Samaria the central highlands, and Gilead the land east of the Jordan. Zarephath lay up the coast in Phoenicia, where Elijah once stayed with a widow (1 Kgs 17:9). Sepharad is a place we cannot identify with certainty; it has often been connected with Sardis in Asia Minor, and Jewish readers in the Middle Ages took it to mean Spain, which is why Jews of Spanish descent are still called Sephardic. The point of the list is not geography but reversal: the people who lost everything will be given more than they lost, and the scattered exiles will come home.

Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

The book ends in one magnificent line. Saviors is the word used for the deliverers God raised up in the days of the judges (Judg 3:9; Neh 9:27): men who rescued his people when they cried to him. They go up to Mount Zion, the hill of God, and from there they rule Mount Esau, the proud height that thought itself untouchable.

And then the closing line, which is the point of the whole book: the kingdom shall be the LORD's. Not Edom's. Not Babylon's. Not any empire, party or power that currently seems to own the future. The kingdom belongs to God, and one day everyone will see it. Zechariah says it too: the LORD will be king over all the earth (Zech 14:9).

The New Testament shows us how it comes about. There is one Savior who went up to Mount Zion, and he is the Lord himself. Jesus Christ was crucified outside Jerusalem, rose, and ascended to reign, and at the end the announcement rings out, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (Rev 11:15). There is an irony worth noticing here. Centuries after Obadiah, a king of Edomite descent, Herod the Great, sat on a throne in Judea and tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matt 2:16). Esau's line made one last attempt on the child of Jacob's line, and failed. Within a century the Edomites had vanished from history; the King they tried to kill reigns forever.

So this little book leaves the believer with three things. Do not be proud, because God brings the high down. Do not gloat over anyone's fall, because God is watching how we treat our brothers. And do not fear the Edoms of this world, however secure they look: the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

1.title: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
1.overview:
Obadiah receives a vision concerning Edom: a report has gone out among the nations, summoning them to battle against her. God will make Edom small and despised (vv. 1-2). The pride of Edom's heart has deceived her; though she lives in the clefts of the rock and nests among the stars, God will bring her down (vv. 3-4). Thieves and grape gatherers leave something behind, but Esau will be stripped bare and his treasures searched out; his allies will drive him to the border and set a trap for him (vv. 5-7). On that day God will destroy the wise men of Edom, and her mighty men will be dismayed (vv. 8-9).

The charge is the violence done to his brother Jacob. On the day strangers carried off Jerusalem's wealth and cast lots for the city, Edom stood aloof and was like one of them (vv. 10-11). Eight commands follow: do not gloat, rejoice or boast over your brother's ruin; do not enter my people's gate, gloat over his disaster or loot his wealth; do not stand at the crossroads to cut off the fugitives or hand over the survivors (vv. 12-14).

For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations, and as Edom has done, it shall be done to her; the nations will drink as she drank on God's holy mountain and be as though they had never been (vv. 15-16). But in Mount Zion there will be those who escape; it will be holy, Jacob will possess his own possessions, and the house of Esau will be stubble before the fire (vv. 17-18). God's people will possess the land on every side, and the exiles will return (vv. 19-20). Saviors will go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's (v. 21).
1.theology:
God rules the nations and moves them as he wills, even when they think they are choosing their own wars (v. 1).

Pride deceives; no fortress, wealth or cleverness can protect anyone from God, who opposes the proud (vv. 3-4, 8-9; Isa 14:13-14; Jas 4:6; Luke 18:14).

God takes wrongs done within the family of his people personally, and counts the bystander among the attackers (vv. 10-11; Luke 10:31-32; 1 John 3:17; Jas 4:17).

Gloating over another's downfall is sin, and it is where cruelty begins (vv. 12-14; Prov 24:17-18).

God repays what people have done, and Christ drank the cup of that judgment in his people's place (vv. 15-16; Matt 7:2; Gal 6:7; Ps 75:8; Matt 26:39; John 18:11).

God preserves a people who escape, and makes Zion holy; believers have come to the heavenly Zion in Christ (v. 17; Joel 2:32; Heb 12:22-24).

Judgment on hostile nations and mercy to individuals from them belong together: a remnant of Edom is promised to the kingdom of David's Son (v. 18; Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16-17).

History ends with salvation on Mount Zion and with God's kingdom, established by Jesus Christ, the true Savior and King (v. 21; Judg 3:9; Zech 14:9; Rev 11:15).
1.examples:
A nation nesting in the cliffs, asking who could ever bring it down.

Thieves who leave something behind, and a judgment that leaves nothing.

Friends at the dinner table setting a trap under the host.

A brother standing at a distance, watching a city burn.

A look that becomes a cheer, a cheer that becomes a robbery.

Refugees caught at the crossroads by the people they ran to for help.

A cup passed round in triumph, and the same cup drunk in judgment.

Dry stubble where a fortress used to be.

Saviors climbing Zion, and a kingdom that belongs to God alone.
